title: Someone Else’s Fault
text: We arrived at the village shortly after that. The liveliness from my last visit was nowhere to be found; a truly gloomy atmosphere hung over the village, and not a single adventurer—of all the many who had been there before—was to be seen. Over at the church, it looked as though a funeral was being held; people with somber expressions appeared to be lowering a coffin into a grave. Then the carriage carrying us entered the village.
“This is… I hope I’m not overstepping, but are you by any chance the Saint of the Divine Bird who visited this village once before?”
“Yes, that’s correct.”
Father, wearing a robe, stepped out of the carriage and replied.
“S-save us, Saint! Please save our village! A plague is currently ravaging this village, and our residents are dying day by day!”
“I know. But…”
The villagers hurried toward where the sick were gathered. At the same time, a man who appeared to be the village chief approached.
“Oh! Holy One! Please save our village!”
“Before that, there’s something I must say.”
“What is it?”
“I want you to fully understand what I said when I left this village… and realize that you brought this upon yourselves.”
In a tone of stern reproach, Father shot a sharp glance at the villagers from beneath the folds of his robe.
“W-well, that—”
“The tavern owner, the person in charge at the giant dragon’s carcass, and you—I warned you all countless times. I won’t let you claim you don’t remember what happened then.”
At Father’s words, the village chief coughed and wiped the sweat from his brow. At the same time, the villagers all turned their gaze toward the village chief.
“Did I say to single out just one person? This is collective responsibility. You should all realize that you’ve brought this upon yourselves.”
“If you let him keep talking, he’ll get too bold! Gah!”

Oh? The man who tried to lunge at my Father coughed up blood. That’s karma for you. That’s exactly why the plague spread. It’s punishment for disregarding the words of my Father, who is as good as a god.
“It seems to be a rather potent plague. If we do nothing… what will become of you all…”
“Oh dear,” my Father murmurs in a tone of lament.
“Well, we’ve come to lend a helping hand to people like you. But I want you to realize this: Who is to blame?　I’ll say it plainly: it’s you yourselves.”

Father feeds a special remedy—one even more potent than the cure—to the unconscious fool lying on the ground. Just that alone calms the fool’s breathing, and his complexion improves before our very eyes.
“Oh… it’s a miracle, just as the rumors said…”
It was clear at a glance that hope was kindling in the villagers’ eyes.
“Holy One! Please, please save our village!”
“Is there really… any value in saving you lot, who’ve grown so accustomed to being given things?”
“How can you say that!”

The villagers were stunned by Father’s ruthless reply. He must be admonishing them so harshly out of concern for the Assistant. After all, the Assistant had asked him to save this village, even though he harbored a grudge against it. So, to prevent this from happening again, Father is issuing this warning on the Assistant’s behalf.
“I’ll say it as many times as it takes. You ignore my advice and seek only profit. Looking objectively at the way you live, do you really think God will bestow His blessings upon you?”
“Oh…”
All the villagers placed their hands over their hearts and bowed their heads toward Father.
“I don’t know what your religion is like, but you must surely have the will to do what is right. Can you say with absolute certainty that this isn’t divine punishment for your arrogance?”
“You are quite right. But… please grant us a reprieve, Holy One!”
“…Hmm. That’s why we came. Now, show us the sick!”
“This way, Holy One.”
Then we were led to an isolated building. Exhausted patients, a brand-new cemetery in the back… I’d say the atmosphere here is even more dire than that of a battlefield.

It reminds me of the relief efforts and funerals held after the battle with the Phoenix. But this place has an even more… gloomy and unpleasant stench than that. It seems even Filolial-sama and the others are repulsed by the smell.

Amidst it all, Father uses his shield skills to treat the patients one after another. Thanks to the specific antidotes he’d prepared in advance, the treatment of the sick progresses swiftly, with the help of the healers present on site.
As the patients begin to recover, Father’s expression grows increasingly grim.
“Even if it’s their own fault, seeing people suffer from illness is painful for the observer, too.”
“I understand how you feel.”

I imagine a plague must have spread in this area in the world before the loop as well. Back then, Father must have come here to save the people, too. Otherwise, the people wouldn’t say that the Shield Hero isn’t a villain. I believe it was thanks to accomplishing these small—yet miraculous—feats that my Father earned the people’s trust and was able to defeat the Three Heroes Church.

However… is this what you’d call the “scent of death”? Breathing in this air—which Filolial-sama so strongly detests—for too long would surely make anyone’s spirits grow gloomy. Since the dragon is the cause, I’d like to dispose of it as soon as possible.
“If only the Sword Hero hadn’t come, this situation wouldn’t have happened…”
My father glared sharply at the villager who muttered this.

“You’re blaming people for turning this into a tourist attraction? After the Sword Hero defeated the dragon, it was you lot who left the carcass lying there, wasn’t it? If you didn’t like it, you should’ve told the Sword Hero to dispose of it!”
“N-no! I’m so sorry!”

My father was fuming, clearly upset that they showed no remorse. On top of it being their own fault, this mentality of trying to shift the blame onto Ren—I feel like I could just burn it all away with Magic and eradicate it completely. Just then, my Assistant, who had been hiding in the carriage, peeked out worriedly.
“You! Aren’t you the Demi-Human girl from the dragon’s lair!”

One of the surviving villagers—who was also an adventurer—pointed at my Assistant. What kind of obvious statement is that? Since my Father, the Holy One of the Divine Bird, took her in, it’s only natural she’s here. Or what? Are you suggesting I’d sell out someone my Father protected? Maybe I really should just get rid of these guys after all.
“Ah…”
“Because of you, the village has ended up in this mess—”
Father reached out and hoisted that survivor up by the collar.
“All right, everyone! Let’s go home.”
“Eh…”
“…It’s really easy to shift the blame onto others, isn’t it? Even if I say I’ll give you a reprieve, this doesn’t bode well for the future.”

“Have you forgotten? I took that child under my protection. I took her in because she had nowhere else to go. Honestly, I could have abandoned you arrogant lot, but that child begged us to save you, so that’s why we came.”
“N-no, stop… please.”
The assistant is pleading with Father, as if the words were being squeezed out of her. Father suddenly let go of the survivor he had been holding aloft.

“Ah… Maybe some people will think—or even say—that the Saint of the Divine Bird is the mastermind behind this incident… what a ridiculous notion. If that’s the case, is it okay if we leave now? Even if things get better for now, the root cause hasn’t been addressed, has it?”
My father crossed his arms and scolded the village representative.
“Hey? What’s the status of the aid from the government? Isn’t this exactly the kind of situation where the Three Heroes Church is supposed to come to the people’s rescue?”
“W-well, that—!”
“Ah… Have they already abandoned us?”
Father was bluffing, but it seems he hit the nail on the head. The villagers remain silent and avert their gaze.
“Well, maybe it’s safer to just leave it alone than to risk it spreading. Those monsters look pretty vicious, too.”
The representative looks away while glancing toward the mountains.
“The treatment isn’t even finished yet, and the root cause hasn’t been eliminated. Also, ask the healers staying here—find out exactly what kind of disease this is.”
